findings.detail: Credentials are taken from the caller (ctx.user), not the booking organizer; when an attendee or team admin adds guests, calendar events on the organizer's calendar cannot be updated. Also the DB update happens before the calendar update, so a failure leaves inconsistent state.

findings.title: Invalid-email error never cleared and empty entries not handled
findings.detail: isInvalidEmail is never reset on successful validation or when the input changes. The initial value is [""] so an empty field fails validation with a confusing message.

findings.title: Error message built with t() of server message and undefined code
findings.detail: The message string is always truthy so the fallback is dead code; it shows 'undefined: ...' when data.code is missing.

findings.title: Team admin check requires both admin AND owner, and attendees may add guests
findings.detail: `isTeamAdmin && isTeamOwner` demands both roles, so it is almost never satisfied for admins (should be OR). Separately, any existing attendee is authorized to add arbitrary guests, so an attendee can trigger emails and calendar updates on the organizer's behalf. Authorization is also decided from an email match rather than a verified identity.

findings.title: Calendar update uses the caller's credentials and user instead of the organizer's
findings.detail: The EventManager is built from the current user and their credentials. If a team admin or attendee performs the action, the organizer's calendar events cannot be updated correctly, or the wrong accounts are touched. The organizer's credentials should be used (booking.user.credentials is already loaded).

findings.title: Emails are sent for guests that were filtered out, and the case is not normalized
findings.detail: `sendAddGuestsEmails` receives the raw `guests` list rather than `uniqueGuests`. Guests whose emails differ only in case from existing attendees or from the blacklist bypass the filter. The blacklist compares the lowercased list to the un-lowercased guest, so mixed-case blacklisted emails get through. The duplicate check is also case-sensitive.

findings.title: Calendar update is not guarded after the DB write; email errors are swallowed
findings.detail: Attendees are persisted before the calendar update, with no transaction or try/catch. If `updateCalendarAttendees` throws, the client gets an error even though the guests are already saved, and a retry then fails with a misleading 'emails must be unique' error. The email failure catch also drops the error object, so the cause is not logged.

findings.title: New and existing guests get swapped emails
findings.detail: New guests receive the generic 'scheduled' email and existing attendees receive the 'guests added' notification. This is plausible, but the sent guest email also bypasses the event type's disable-standard-emails metadata. The organizer email is also sent unconditionally without checking `eventTypeDisableHostEmail`.

findings.title: Client validation allows empty entries or an empty array to pass
findings.detail: The initial value is `[""]`, and `z.string().email()` rejects empty strings, so removing all rows leaves an empty array and the Add button silently does nothing. The `length === 0` early return gives no feedback. `isInvalidEmail` is also never reset after a successful validation or a later edit.

findings.title: Error toast builds a message that is always truthy and translates server text
findings.detail: The template string always yields a non-empty value, so the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback is dead. It also passes arbitrary server error messages (e.g. Zod validation JSON) through `t()` and prefixes them with the error code.

findings.title: Possible TypeError when destinationCalendar is empty or null
findings.detail: `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is destructured from `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []`, so it is undefined when the array is empty or null. Accessing `.integration` without optional chaining throws, and this path now occurs for every Google Meet booking without a destination calendar.

findings.title: updateEvent fallback compares externalId with the falsy externalCalendarId
findings.detail: This branch only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so `find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` can never match a real calendar and yields undefined. The previous fallback to the destination calendar's externalId is lost, so updates go to the wrong or no calendar.

findings.title: deleteEvent fallback never matches a destination calendar
findings.detail: The ternary's else branch runs only when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so the `find` compares against a falsy value and yields undefined. The deletion then falls back to the default 'primary' calendar instead of the destination calendar.

findings.title: Collective team destination calendars pushed onto possibly null array
findings.detail: `evt.destinationCalendar` is null when neither the event type nor the organizer has one, so `?.push` silently drops the teamDestinationCalendars. Team members' calendars are then never used for collective events. Also, the array is populated as a side effect inside an async map callback.

findings.title: Non-calendar results lose credentialId
findings.detail: For non-calendar results `credentialId` is now always undefined instead of `result.credentialId`. Video and other references therefore lose their credential link, which breaks later update and delete operations.

findings.title: Merged-booking path deletes only the first old calendar reference
findings.detail: Calendar references are now collected as an array and updated in a loop. The old-event deletion logic when merging bookings still handles only the first reference via `find`, so the other calendar events are left behind.

findings.title: loadUsers behavior changed: throws for empty dynamic list and drops organization select
findings.detail: A new throw on an empty `dynamicUserList` turns what was an empty result into an error that is rewrapped as a 500. The `organization` select was removed, which later code that reads `user.organization` may depend on. Fallback `eventType.users` can also be undefined.
findings.evidence: throw new Error("dynamicUserList is not properly defined or empty.");

findings.title: Slug condition inverted
findings.detail: The slug was previously set when billing was NOT enabled, and `requestedSlug` was set when billing was enabled. The change flips the first condition, so the slug is now set only when billing is enabled and orgs created without billing get no slug. This is unrelated to the PR's purpose.

findings.title: Crash when destinationCalendar is empty: destructured element is undefined
findings.detail: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` yields undefined for empty/null arrays, and `.integration` is accessed without optional chaining. Any Google Meet booking with no destination calendar throws a TypeError.

findings.title: updateEvent fallback searches by the externalCalendarId that is already falsy
findings.detail: In the else branch externalCalendarId is falsy, so `find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` never matches a real calendar and returns undefined. The fallback to the event's destination calendar is effectively dead and the update targets an undefined calendar.

findings.title: deleteEvent fallback has same self-defeating lookup
findings.detail: When externalCalendarId is falsy, the fallback finds a calendar whose externalId equals that falsy value, so it returns undefined. Previously the destination calendar's externalId was used.

findings.title: Push onto possibly-null destinationCalendar drops team calendars
findings.detail: destinationCalendar is set to null when neither the event type nor the organizer has one, so `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)` silently does nothing and collective team members' calendars are not added. Also the same-credential DestinationCalendar of the organizer may be duplicated.

findings.title: Reschedule uses references filter but merged old-event deletion and 'other_calendar' paths still single-reference
findings.detail: The loop calls updateEvent for credentials that may be undefined when a credential isn't found in DB (credential stays undefined) and pushes the call anyway, which will crash in updateEvent via credential.appName. Only references with matching credentials should be processed.

findings.title: Error log removed in updateAllCalendarEvents catch
findings.detail: The console.error(message) was dropped, so the formatted failure message built just above is now unused and failures are swallowed silently.

findings.title: loadUsers rewrite drops organization select and throws for empty dynamic list
findings.detail: The organization slug select was removed from the dynamic user query, and loading now throws if dynamicUserList is empty. The eventType.users fallback no longer defaults to []. Code relying on user.organization may break.

findings.title: Inverted slug condition for organization creation
findings.detail: The original set slug when billing is NOT enabled; the change inverts it to set slug when billing IS enabled, and requestedSlug when enabled too. This changes behavior unrelated to this PR and contradicts the intended flow.

findings.title: Null deref when destinationCalendar is empty/null in Meet fallback
findings.detail: `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` when `evt.destinationCalendar` is null or empty, so `.integration` throws a TypeError. Any Google Meet booking without a destination calendar now crashes instead of falling back to Cal Video.

findings.title: Fallback lookup compares externalId to itself, always yields undefined
findings.detail: This branch only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so `find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` can never match a real calendar. The destination calendar fallback is lost and updates/deletes no longer target the destination calendar.

findings.title: Delete fallback calendar lookup is always empty
findings.detail: The same self-comparison against a falsy `externalCalendarId` means the fallback never resolves to a destination calendar. Deletion then goes to the default calendar instead.

findings.title: credentialId/externalId written from createEvent result may be wrong for non-calendar paths
findings.detail: For non-calendar results `credentialId` is set to undefined for the first path, dropping the video credential ID that was previously saved (`result.credentialId`). This loses the credential link for video references.

findings.title: Per-destination externalId not set when no credentialId on destination
findings.detail: In the else-branch of createAllCalendarEvents, `createEvent(c, event)` is called without externalId, so the booking reference's externalCalendarId becomes undefined. This also creates events for every matching credential in each destination, and on later update/delete the right calendar isn't known.

findings.title: Pushing to destinationCalendar may fail when it is null
findings.detail: `evt.destinationCalendar` can be null when there is no event type or organizer destination calendar. Team members' calendars are then silently dropped (optional chaining no-ops), so collective events lose the other hosts' calendars.

findings.title: Inverted slug condition for organization creation
findings.detail: The original set `slug` when team billing was NOT enabled (and requestedSlug when enabled). The change inverts this, so with billing disabled the org gets no slug and with billing enabled it gets both slug and requestedSlug, bypassing the intended approval flow.

findings.title: Credential fetched from DB without ownership check; undefined credential passed to updateEvent
findings.detail: A credential id from a booking reference is fetched by id from the DB without checking it belongs to the user or team, and if lookup fails `credential` may stay undefined (or stale from the previous loop iteration) and is still passed to updateEvent.

findings.title: Recurring deletion repeated for every calendar reference
findings.detail: Inside the per-reference loop, the recurring branch deletes events across all of the user's calendar credentials for all updated bookings. With multiple references this repeats the same deletions N times.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with !== on header, can be bypassed or timing-leaked
findings.detail: The header is compared to process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET with a plain inequality, which is not constant-time. The enabled flag only requires the secret to be truthy, but the header could be an array or the header name misconfigured. A non-timing-safe comparison allows secret recovery by timing.

findings.title: Computed zod keys are bogus; schema does not do what comment says
findings.detail: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to a fixed string like "[object Object]" (or ZodString's toString), so it creates a required literal property with that name. The schema therefore requires a nonexistent key and every sync-mode parse fails; it does not mean 'any numeric property is the expiry'.

findings.title: parseRefreshTokenResponse result used as the credential key
findings.detail: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a SafeParse result object ({success, data}), not the parsed data. Storing it as `key` writes {success:true,data:{...}} into the credential, corrupting the Google credential. It also parses the stale googleCredentials rather than the refresh response.

findings.title: Salesforce token is refreshed on every connection without checking expiry
findings.detail: A refresh request is made unconditionally each time a connection is created, adding a network call and risking rate limits. The new salesforceTokenSchema also requires fields such as id and signature that a refresh response may not contain, so parsing throws. The check `!accessTokenParsed.success` is dead since the function throws instead of returning.

findings.title: Sync endpoint response is not parsed or compatible with callers' expected shapes
findings.detail: The sync-endpoint branch returns a raw fetch Response, while the fallback returns provider-specific objects (axios response, Google res, hubspot token). Callers like zoho/bigin read `.data` and Hubspot/Google use the result directly, so they break when sync is enabled. There is also no authentication header or response status check on the request.

findings.title: credentialId passed where userId is expected
findings.detail: refreshOAuthTokens takes a userId, but the credential id is passed. When sync is on, the sync endpoint gets the wrong user identifier and fetches/returns tokens for the wrong user.

findings.title: Unhandled zod parse and JSON/decrypt errors
findings.detail: The body is parsed with .parse(), which throws on invalid input, and JSON.parse/symmetricDecrypt can also throw, producing 500s instead of 400s. The decrypt key falls back to an empty string.

findings.title: Result of parseRefreshTokenResponse used with .success but it now throws
findings.detail: parseRefreshTokenResponse throws on invalid input, so the old error logging is removed and failure now propagates as a generic error. Also `refresh_token` is set to the literal 'refresh_token' when missing, which could overwrite a real stored refresh token.

findings.title: Placeholder refresh token written into data
findings.detail: When the response has no refresh_token, the string "refresh_token" is injected as a fake value, and it gets persisted in credentials for providers whose normal schema omits it, replacing a valid token.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with !== and may be undefined or non-string
findings.detail: The header value is compared to process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET with a non-constant-time comparison. The header can also be an array. Timing leaks allow secret guessing. Anyone who passes this check can overwrite any user's credentials.

findings.title: Credential ID passed as userId to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.detail: refreshOAuthTokens expects the Cal.com userId, but credentialId is passed. With credential sync enabled, the sync endpoint is asked for the wrong user's tokens, which can return another user's token and corrupt the credential. The response is also a fetch Response, not an axios result, so tokenInfo.data is undefined.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh logic misuses parseRefreshTokenResponse and always refreshes
findings.detail: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a safeParse result and throws on failure, and the salesforce schema requires fields a refresh response may lack. The token refresh now runs on every connection creation with no expiry check and bypasses refreshOAuthTokens. It also calls prisma.credential.update with the parsed result's data even if a sync flow was intended.

findings.title: Google key stored as safeParse result object instead of data
findings.detail: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a zod SafeParseReturnType ({success,data}). It is saved directly as the credential key, which corrupts the stored credential. The old code stored the parsed data. The input is also googleCredentials, not the token response.

findings.title: Computed zod keys are meaningless
findings.detail: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to a literal string such as '[object Object]' or 'ZodString', not a wildcard key. The schema therefore requires a bogus property and rejects real token responses. The code also overwrites a missing refresh_token with the literal 'refresh_token'.

findings.title: Dead success check and removed error logging after parse now throws
findings.detail: parseRefreshTokenResponse throws on failure and always returns a success result, so `tokenResponse.success && ...` is redundant. The removed error log is replaced by a generic throw that drops the Microsoft error context.

findings.title: Unhandled zod parse and JSON/decrypt errors
findings.detail: parse() throws on invalid body, and JSON.parse/symmetricDecrypt can throw on bad ciphertext, producing 500s instead of 400s. The encryption key falls back to an empty string when unset.

findings.title: Sync endpoint request has no authentication or error handling
findings.detail: The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends no secret or auth header and no content type. Callers treat the returned fetch Response as the provider's native result (e.g. hubspot, axios callers read .data). Several callers will break.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean
findings.detail: The constant is the result of `&&` between env strings, so it is a string or undefined rather than a boolean. Without `!!` it leaks the secret value into the exported constant and misleads type consumers.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with !== and no timing safety; undefined header may match
findings.detail: The header value is compared with plain `!==` against the secret, which is not constant-time. The secret is only checked for truthiness via the combined constant, so a mismatch of types (array header values) is not handled either. Use crypto.timingSafeEqual and require a string header.

findings.title: Unhandled zod parse / decrypt / JSON.parse errors and no method check
findings.detail: `.parse` throws on invalid body, and symmetricDecrypt/JSON.parse can throw on bad input, producing 500s instead of 400 responses. The handler also accepts any HTTP method.

findings.title: Computed zod keys are bogus; minimum schema is broken
findings.detail: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to a fixed string like "[object Object]" (ZodString toString), so the schema requires a nonexistent numeric property. When sync is enabled, every refresh response fails validation and throws, or the intended any-number/passthrough behavior is never achieved.

findings.title: Placeholder refresh_token written into credential
findings.detail: If the response has no refresh_token, it is set to the literal "refresh_token" and may be stored in the credential, overwriting a valid refresh token with garbage in the normal (non-sync) path too.

findings.title: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a SafeParse result, stored as key
findings.detail: The function returns the safeParse result object ({success,data}) not the parsed data, so `key` saved to the DB is the wrapper object rather than the credentials. Also it parses googleCredentials rather than the refresh response.

findings.title: Salesforce always refreshes token on every connection, bypassing sync, and with response.statusText check
findings.detail: A token refresh request is made unconditionally each time a connection is created (not through refreshOAuthTokens), rewriting the credential with the response data on each call. The statusText check ('OK') is fragile (empty under HTTP/2).
findings.evidence: if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw new HttpError({ statusCode: 400, message: response.statusText });

findings.title: credentialId passed where userId expected
findings.detail: refreshOAuthTokens expects the user ID, but the credential's id is passed, so the sync endpoint would be queried with the wrong user.

findings.title: Sync endpoint fetch unauthenticated, no response status check
findings.detail: The POST to the sync endpoint sends no authentication/secret and the response is returned without checking status; callers then parse the body as a provider token response. Failures are not handled.

findings.title: safeParse result used after parse now throws; dead success check and lost error logging
findings.detail: parseRefreshTokenResponse throws on failure, making `tokenResponse.success` checks redundant, and the previous console.error diagnostic was removed.

findings.title: Caching tests removed although caching logic still exists
findings.detail: The 'Caching' describe block was deleted, but getAuthorizationConditions and getFilterConditions still memoize via cachedAuthConditions and cachedFilterConditions. Nothing now verifies that the cached Prisma.Sql is reused, so a regression in that logic would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Constructor options type loosened so team scope no longer requires teamId
findings.detail: InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions makes teamId optional for every scope. A caller can pass scope 'team' without teamId and it compiles. At runtime zod validation fails and options become null, so the service silently returns the NOTHING condition (no rows) instead of surfacing the misuse.

findings.title: Unparenthesized OR filter can break AND precedence with other filters
findings.detail: The eventTypeId condition is built as `(a) OR (b)` without outer parentheses. When it is the only filter it is returned raw; getBaseConditions wraps it, but any caller or later combination that composes it without wrapping would let OR bind incorrectly. Wrap the sub-condition in parentheses.

findings.title: Org scope drops user condition when org has no child teams
findings.detail: userIdsFromOrg is only fetched when teamsFromOrg.length > 0, so for an org without child teams, members of the org itself are never included in the user clause, though teamIds contains the orgId. This was pre-existing but retained in the new SQL path.
findings.evidence: const conditions: Prisma.Sql[] = [Prisma.sql`("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)`];

findings.title: Tests compare Prisma.Sql objects structurally, brittle and not validating behavior
findings.detail: Tests assert equality of Sql objects rather than executing the query. The only executed test covers just the user scope and eventTypeId filter, leaving the org/team OR conditions and ANY array behavior unexecuted against the DB. Removed caching tests also leave caching untested.

findings.title: updateMany with empty data does not bump updatedAt
findings.detail: Prisma's updateMany with an empty data object issues no UPDATE, so @updatedAt is not refreshed. The comment says updatedAt is updated for all calendars, but this is effectively a no-op (extra query at best).

findings.title: Ownership check excludes team/delegation credentials and uses a generic Error
findings.detail: The handler only matches credentials where userId equals the caller, so legitimate delegation credentials are rejected. A plain Error is thrown instead of a TRPCError, so the client sees an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR rather than a NOT_FOUND or FORBIDDEN response.
findings.evidence: throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied");

findings.title: Dropdown item containing nested button/interactive content and non-actionable cache status item
findings.detail: The cache status entry is a DropdownMenuItem with no action, and a DropdownItem button is nested inside DropdownMenuItem, which creates nested interactive elements. Cache status should be a label.

findings.title: Uses real CalendarCacheRepository regardless of cache feature flag
findings.detail: A mock repository exists for when calendar-cache is disabled, but the handler always queries the DB through the real repository. This adds a groupBy query on every connectedCalendars call even when the feature is off.

findings.title: Empty update does not bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt reliably
findings.detail: The comment says it updates SelectedCalendar.updatedAt, but it passes an empty data object `{}`. Prisma's updateMany with no data fields may not set @updatedAt, so the timestamp may never change. The call also runs one extra write on every cache-refresh run.

findings.title: Cache deletion only authorized for credentials owned directly by user
findings.detail: The ownership check only matches `userId: user.id`. The UI shows the cache menu for delegation credentials, which are in-memory with negative ids, so deletion fails for those users. Failures throw a plain Error, which tRPC surfaces as an internal server error rather than a NOT_FOUND or FORBIDDEN TRPCError.
findings.evidence: throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied");

findings.title: Cache delete option gated by cache existence and Google type; no modification guard
findings.detail: `hasCache` ignores `disableConnectionModification`, so a user who should not modify the connection can still delete cached data. `hasCache` also evaluates to a Date or null rather than a boolean and is used in JSX with `&&`.

findings.title: Nested interactive elements inside DropdownMenuItem
findings.detail: A DropdownItem (button) is nested inside a DropdownMenuItem, so Radix treats the outer item as the interactive element. This produces invalid nested interactive markup and can leave the dropdown menu focus and close behaviour broken. The cache status item also behaves as a clickable menu item although it is informational.

findings.title: macOS-only sed -i '' breaks on Linux
findings.detail: `sed -i ''` is BSD/macOS syntax. On GNU sed it treats '' as the script and fails, so the env file is never updated on Linux. Also ENV_FILE is a relative path (../.env) that depends on the current working directory.

findings.title: Script exits with status 0 on failures
findings.detail: cleanup always calls `exit 0`, including the rate-limit and URL-extraction failure paths, so callers cannot detect failure. The rate-limit check inside the loop is also only reachable when tmole is not already running.

findings.title: Empty updateMany relies on @updatedAt, which Prisma does not apply for empty data
findings.detail: Calling updateMany with `{}` does not reliably bump `updatedAt`, because Prisma may skip the update when there is no data. The intended "touch" of SelectedCalendar.updatedAt may never happen. It also updates every selected calendar for the credential on each call, including eventType-level ones.

findings.title: Cache deletion only authorizes credentials owned directly by the user
findings.detail: The ownership check requires credential.userId === user.id. Delegation credentials are shown in the UI with the cache option, but their credentialId is in-memory and negative. Deleting their cache will always fail with a generic error. Team-owned credentials are likewise unsupported.

findings.title: Plain Error thrown instead of TRPCError
findings.detail: A generic Error becomes an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR response rather than NOT_FOUND or FORBIDDEN. This misreports an authorization failure and gives clients the wrong status.
findings.evidence: throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied");

findings.title: Cache status shown as dropdown menu item that closes the menu on click
findings.detail: The read-only status text is wrapped in a DropdownMenuItem, so clicking it selects and closes the menu. It is also formatted with a hardcoded en-US locale instead of the user's locale.

findings.title: Extra cache query always run, even when calendar cache is disabled
findings.detail: The handler always instantiates the real CalendarCacheRepository and runs a groupBy query on every connectedCalendars call. The mock repository designed for the disabled-cache case is bypassed. The query also includes negative in-memory delegation credential ids.

findings.title: BSD-only sed -i syntax breaks on Linux
findings.detail: `sed -i ''` works on macOS only. On GNU sed the empty string is treated as the script argument and the command fails. ENV_FILE is also a relative path that depends on the current working directory.

findings.title: Eager dynamic imports defeat lazy loading and add unhandled-rejection risk
findings.detail: Each `import()` in the object literal runs at module load, so every app is loaded immediately rather than on demand. The promises are also created without any rejection handler; if a single app module fails to load, that causes an unhandled rejection and every awaiting caller is affected.

findings.title: async forEach callback: deletions not awaited, errors escape try/catch
findings.detail: forEach does not await the async callback. The try/catch cannot catch rejections from getCalendar or deleteEvent, which become unhandled rejections. The function proceeds to send emails and return before calendar and video deletions finish.

findings.title: async forEach callback: deletions not awaited, errors escape try/catch
findings.detail: The async callback passed to forEach is not awaited, so deletion failures bypass the surrounding try/catch and become unhandled rejections. The reschedule flow returns before the calendar events are actually deleted.

findings.title: async forEach in requestReschedule leaves deletions unawaited
findings.detail: The async forEach callback is not awaited. Calendar deletions may not finish before the mutation responds, and any rejection is unhandled. In serverless runtimes the work can be cut off entirely.

findings.title: Recurring cancellation deletes run in unawaited async forEach
findings.detail: The callback awaits getCalendar and deleteEvent, but forEach does not wait for it. The Promise.all(apiDeletes) later runs before the deletions complete. Results are pushed into apiDeletes after it has been consumed, and errors are unhandled.

findings.title: getCalendarCredentials stores un-awaited Promises as calendar
findings.detail: getCalendar is now async, so `calendar` in getCalendarCredentials is a Promise. Other consumers of getCalendarCredentials' `.calendar` that expect a Calendar or null get a Promise, which is always truthy, so null checks pass and method calls fail.

findings.title: async forEach callback makes try/catch ineffective and deletions unawaited
findings.detail: forEach does not await the async callback. The returned promises are dropped, so the try/catch never catches rejections (unhandled rejection). Calendar and video deletes may not finish before the function returns or the request ends.

findings.title: async forEach callback makes try/catch ineffective and deletions unawaited
findings.detail: The async callback inside forEach is never awaited, so errors from getCalendar/deleteEvent become unhandled rejections instead of being logged. Deletion work may be abandoned or race with the response.

findings.title: async forEach in reschedule request not awaited
findings.detail: Calendar deletions are run in an async forEach callback. The mutation proceeds without waiting, and rejections are unhandled and not caught by surrounding error handling.

findings.title: Recurring cancel deletes pushed after async forEach, not awaited
findings.detail: The forEach callback is async and now awaits getCalendar before deleteEvent. apiDeletes.push occurs after Promise.all(apiDeletes) has already run, so the recurring event deletions are not awaited and may be lost or unhandled.

findings.title: All app modules eagerly imported at module load via import()
findings.detail: Each property calls import() immediately when the module is evaluated, so every app is loaded at startup. This is not lazy loading and is unnecessary overhead. A single failing import also creates an unhandled rejected promise.

findings.title: Eager dynamic imports make lazy loading a no-op and can create import cycles
findings.detail: Each property is `import(...)` evaluated immediately when the module loads, so all ~29 apps are loaded at startup (not lazily). Any one failing import produces a rejected promise held in the object for every consumer.

findings.title: async forEach callback makes try/catch ineffective and calendar deletion unawaited
findings.detail: The async callback returns promises that forEach ignores, so the try/catch can't catch failures (unhandled rejections) and emails are sent before deletions finish. Before this change, sync errors were caught.

findings.title: async forEach callback makes try/catch ineffective and deletion unawaited
findings.detail: Calendar and video deletions are fire-and-forget; rejected promises become unhandled rejections and the try/catch no longer protects, and the function returns before deletes complete.

findings.title: async forEach in reschedule request leaves deletions unawaited
findings.detail: The async callback inside forEach isn't awaited, so calendar/video deletions may not complete before the response or may fail with unhandled rejections that are not caught by the surrounding try/catch.

findings.title: Async forEach pushes into apiDeletes after it has been awaited
findings.detail: The forEach callback is now async and awaits getCalendar; the deleteEvent promises are pushed to apiDeletes after `Promise.all(apiDeletes)` may already have run, so recurring calendar deletions are not awaited and errors go unhandled.

findings.title: Default `queued` timestamp evaluated once at import time
findings.detail: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the class is defined, so every AssignmentSource shares the process start time as its `queued` value. It should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

findings.title: to_dict yields a datetime that cannot be serialized for the Celery task
findings.detail: `asdict` keeps `queued` as a datetime object. It is passed in the kwargs of `apply_async`, and a JSON serializer will fail or turn it into a string. `from_dict` then builds the dataclass with a string `queued` value, which is not a datetime.

findings.title: from_dict silently swallows parse failures
findings.detail: On invalid input `from_dict` returns None with no log. The task then treats it as having no source and syncs outbound. Cycle protection is disabled without anyone noticing.

findings.title: Default `queued` timestamp evaluated once at import time
findings.detail: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated when the class is defined, so every AssignmentSource without an explicit value gets the same stale process-start timestamp. It needs `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

findings.title: to_dict yields a datetime that is not JSON-serializable for the task queue
findings.detail: `asdict` keeps `queued` as a datetime object. This dict is passed as a kwarg to `apply_async`, and Celery's JSON serializer may fail or turn it into a string. If it becomes a string, `from_dict` accepts it silently and the type no longer matches.

findings.title: from_dict failure silently drops the sync-cycle guard
findings.detail: When `from_dict` fails and returns None, the task treats the call as having no source. The outbound sync then runs and re-creates the cycle the check exists to prevent. The failure is not logged.

findings.title: Default `queued` timestamp evaluated once at import time
findings.detail: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated when the class is defined, so every AssignmentSource that does not pass `queued` shares the process-start time. The field is meant to record when the assignment was queued, so the stored value is wrong. It needs `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

findings.title: Non-JSON-serializable datetime passed in Celery task kwargs
findings.detail: `assignment_source.to_dict()` uses `asdict`, which leaves `queued` as a datetime object. This dict is passed as Celery kwargs. With the JSON serializer, enqueueing fails or the value is stringified. After a round trip, `from_dict` would receive a string rather than a datetime.

findings.title: Working-hours check uses same value for start and end, wrongly filters slots
findings.detail: `end` is computed identically to `start` and not offset by event length. Also, working hours are in minutes in the organizer's timezone, but the slot is compared in UTC without conversion. Any slot outside a single working-hour entry of any matching day is rejected, so slots can be wrongly dropped, and the `end > endTime` check can never reflect the slot end.

findings.title: Working-hours `find` returns true when any one entry excludes the slot
findings.detail: With multiple working-hour ranges on the same day (e.g. 9-12 and 13-17), a slot inside one range is still outside the other, so `find` matches and the slot is rejected as outside working hours. This incorrectly removes valid slots for split schedules.

findings.title: Dayjs objects compared by reference with ===
findings.detail: Two new dayjs objects are compared with `===`, which is always false, so the zero-length override branch is dead code. Should use isSame.

findings.title: Override day match compares UTC-shifted override date against UTC slot date, and ignores the slot end
findings.detail: The override date is shifted by the negated organizer offset, and `dayjs.tz(date.start, tz).utcOffset()` is evaluated for the wrong instant. Slots that cross the override end are not rejected (only slotStart after end is checked, not slotEnd), and slots on non-overridden dates of other users are treated by the aggregated date match inconsistently.

findings.title: Override offset computed from stringified Date and applied to UTC wall time
findings.detail: `override.start.toString()` yields a locale string that dayjs parses in the server's local zone, which is fragile. `override.timeZone` can be undefined (optional), causing `.tz(undefined)` to use the local zone. Also the hour/minute wraparound across midnight is lost when offset shifts the time past a day boundary.

findings.title: Working-hours check uses identical start and end, and wrong comparison basis
findings.detail: `end` is computed identically to `start` (slot start, not slot end), so the end-of-day check never accounts for event length. Also workingHour times are in the organizer's timezone-serialized form but compared to UTC slot hour/minute. Slots can run past working hours or valid slots get rejected.

findings.title: Working-hours rejection logic marks slot unavailable if any single window excludes it
findings.detail: `find` returns true when the slot is outside ANY working-hour entry for that day. Users with multiple windows (e.g. 9-12 and 14-18) will have every slot rejected because it is outside the other window. Needs `some` inside-check negated over all windows.

findings.title: Dayjs objects compared with === (always false)
findings.detail: Comparing two distinct Dayjs object instances with `===` is always false, so the zero-length override (day off) branch never triggers.

findings.title: Override date matching and offset sign/usage are inconsistent and fragile
findings.detail: The utcOffset is computed via dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone) which reinterprets the Date in the tz and negates it. Date overrides are matched by the UTC day of the slot, which breaks for overrides near midnight or other timezones. The slot-start-after-end check also ignores event length (slotEnd after override end is allowed).

findings.title: Slot overrunning override end is not rejected
findings.detail: Only slotStartTime.isAfter(override end) is checked, so a slot that starts before the end but whose end extends past the override end is accepted.

findings.title: Date converted via toString() and possibly undefined timezone
findings.detail: `override.start.toString()` yields a locale-format string that dayjs parses non-deterministically; `override.timeZone` is optional and `.tz(undefined)` falls back to local tz, giving wrong offsets. Offset also uses override start's offset for end.

findings.title: New test uses UTC-day range that doesn't match +6:00 timezone
findings.detail: The request range is for +5:30 day boundaries (18:30Z) but is passed with the +6:00 timezone, and the custom matcher only checks returned slots against expected index-wise (no length check), so the test is weak.

findings.title: Working-hours check compares start to itself, wrong end and unit mismatch
findings.detail: `end` is computed identically to `start`, so the end check never reflects slot end. Also, workingHours startTime/endTime are minutes in the organizer's timezone but are compared to the slot's UTC hour/minute, which wrongly rejects valid slots. The lambda also returns true for any matching entry that is out of range, so with multiple working-hour blocks on the same day (e.g., split shifts) a slot inside one block is rejected because it is outside another.

findings.title: Dayjs object compared with === is always false
findings.detail: Comparing two distinct dayjs instances using === is never true, so this zero-length-override branch is dead code. It should use isSame or compare valueOf.

findings.title: Override check rejects slots based on wrong conditions and sign of offset
findings.detail: The override branches return true (meaning 'slot is outside override') when the slot ends before/at override start or starts after override end, but a slot that overruns the override end is not rejected. The date match uses the override's offset applied to date.start in a questionable way (dayjs.tz(Date, tz) offset, negated), and the sameness of date format compares only day. The offset sign and the use of the override's own date may misclassify slots near midnight.

findings.title: Early return skips busy-time check when a date override exists
findings.detail: When a date override covers the slot, the function returns true before evaluating the busy times, so slots in conflict with bookings or calendar busy periods on override days are reported as available (double booking).

findings.title: Override offset computed using possibly undefined timezone and string conversion
findings.detail: override.timeZone is optional; dayjs.tz(undefined) falls back to local timezone, giving wrong offsets. Also `override.start.toString()` produces a locale-formatted string parse, which is non-ISO and error-prone; also the hour/minute extraction is repeated.

findings.title: Email reminders with a referenceId are only flagged, never removed from the DB on default path
findings.detail: In the default (non-immediate) path, scheduled email reminders are only marked cancelled=true and rely on the cron to cancel them, but the cron only picks cancelled reminders due within 1 hour, and an earlier cron step deletes all EMAIL reminders whose scheduledDate is past. Reminders scheduled further out stay in SendGrid and send as normal until the cron runs within the 1 hour window. Meanwhile the booking attendee/references are deleted, and the reminders remain active for up to 72 hours.

findings.title: immediateDelete path cancels in SendGrid but never deletes the DB reminder
findings.detail: When immediateDelete is true, the batch is cancelled in SendGrid and the function returns without removing the WorkflowReminder row. The row stays forever and the cron deletes later; workflow/step deletion paths rely on cascade, but the reschedule path in handleNewBooking leaves stale rows. The prior SendGrid DELETE of the batch id was also dropped.

findings.title: Cron cancel loop aborts all remaining cancellations on first failure and doesn't filter by method
findings.detail: The findMany does not filter by method EMAIL, and a single failing SendGrid request throws out of the loop, skipping the rest and leaving the earlier-created delete promises unawaited. Note also the prisma delete calls are PrismaPromise built lazily and only executed on await after the loop. Rows with null referenceId would send an invalid batch_id.

findings.title: try/catch around async delete calls cannot catch errors; promises are not awaited
findings.detail: deleteScheduledEmailReminder/SMS are async and invoked without await inside forEach, so the try/catch is ineffective and the deletions race with the rest of the booking flow (floating promises).

findings.title: Reminder deletion not awaited; removed from the Promise.all
findings.detail: Reminder cancellation calls are fire-and-forget and no longer part of prismaPromises, so the handler can return (serverless) before the DB updates/Twilio cancellations complete, and failures are silently lost.

findings.title: Unrelated reformatting corrupts commented block indentation and imports lack trailing comma
findings.detail: A commented-out code block was de-indented, adding noise, and imports changed from type-only to value imports of Prisma/PrismaPromise, which are now unused (PrismaPromise, Prisma) after the refactor.

findings.title: Non-immediate email cancel only flags row; scheduled email can still send
findings.detail: By default (no immediateDelete) a reminder with a referenceId is only marked cancelled=true. The cron only cancels those due within the next hour, and SendGrid only accepts cancellation of batches scheduled up to 72h out. Meanwhile the cron's first step deletes every EMAIL reminder whose scheduledDate is past, and the flagged row remains until then, so cancellations can be lost. For cancel and reschedule flows, the email can still be sent.

findings.title: immediateDelete cancels in SendGrid but never deletes the DB row
findings.detail: With immediateDelete=true the function sends the cancel request and returns, so the WorkflowReminder row stays in the database. The previous code also called DELETE on the scheduled send. Callers such as workflow deletion and step removal expect the reminder to be removed. Stale rows remain, and the cron can later try to cancel them again.

findings.title: Cron cancel loop is not per-item safe and queries all methods
findings.detail: The query for cancelled reminders has no method filter, so cancelled SMS rows or rows with a null referenceId are also sent to SendGrid. A single failing request aborts the whole try block and skips deleting the remaining rows. Failed items are therefore retried forever. The loop also awaits sequentially.

findings.title: Async reminder deletion not awaited; try/catch ineffective
findings.detail: deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async, but the calls are not awaited, so the surrounding try/catch catches nothing. The deletions race with the later reschedule logic and run as unawaited promises.

findings.title: Rescheduled booking: SMS deleted but email DB rows retained
findings.detail: On reschedule, email reminders use immediateDelete=true, which cancels in SendGrid but leaves the DB row. The row is only removed later by the cron's past-date cleanup. Meanwhile the old booking's rows remain and are inconsistent with the SMS handling.

findings.title: Reminder cancellations are fire-and-forget and not awaited
findings.detail: The async delete helpers are invoked inside forEach without being awaited or added to prismaPromises. The DB updates and deletes may not finish before the response, and in serverless environments they can be cut off. The previous code awaited the DB deleteMany promises.

findings.title: Unnecessary async forEach callback and value imports of types
findings.detail: The edited-steps loop is still `forEach(async ...)` yet awaits nothing, and the deletions run unawaited. PrismaPromise and Prisma are now imported as values although they are only used as types.

findings.title: Email reminders with referenceId are only flagged cancelled, never cancelled in SendGrid
findings.detail: In the default path (immediateDelete falsy) a scheduled reminder with a referenceId is only marked cancelled=true. The cron only cancels those whose scheduledDate is within the next hour, but SendGrid batches are scheduled up to 72h ahead and may send before the cron processes them. Also, scheduleEmailReminders first deletes all EMAIL reminders with scheduledDate <= now, so only reminders in a narrow window are cancelled.

findings.title: immediateDelete cancels in SendGrid but leaves the DB reminder row
findings.detail: When immediateDelete is true the SendGrid batch is cancelled and the function returns without deleting the WorkflowReminder row. The orphaned row remains scheduled=true, and the old DELETE of the scheduled_send is also gone, so cancelled batches stay in SendGrid. For reschedules, the booking is not deleted, so rows persist.

findings.title: Cron cancellation query is not restricted to EMAIL and the loop aborts on first failure
findings.detail: The findMany for cancelled reminders does not filter on method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL, and the try/catch wraps the whole loop so one failing SendGrid request stops the rest. Also reminders whose referenceId is null are sent to SendGrid with batch_id null. Deletes are queued as lazy Prisma promises and only run at Promise.all after all requests.

findings.title: Async reminder deletion is fire-and-forget and not awaited
findings.detail: deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder now perform DB writes but are not awaited or added to prismaPromises, which previously were awaited. In serverless handlers the work may be dropped after the response. The booking deletion cascade may also race with the reminder delete, producing errors.

findings.title: Unguarded metadata['sender']['login'] access can raise KeyError
findings.detail: `sender` is only stored in metadata when the state contains it (`if state.get("sender")`). For integrations created without a sender (older ones or ones missing the webhook), this lookup raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of a controlled error.

findings.title: Token exchange and user-info calls are not guarded against failures
findings.detail: safe_urlopen sits outside the try block, and get_user_info is unguarded. Network errors raise unhandled exceptions (500) instead of showing the friendly error page. Also, the returned `code` may be None when the callback is missing it.

findings.title: Flow skips sender check when Integration does not exist, and check is outside OAuth state handling
findings.detail: When the Integration does not yet exist, the sender check is skipped, so any authenticated GitHub user can claim an installation id that has no Integration yet. Authorization is therefore only enforced for pre-existing integrations.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer verifies the 404 installation-not-found path
findings.detail: The test now asserts the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message, which results from a state mismatch (a hardcoded wrong state), not from the installation lookup failing. The 404 handling in build_integration is no longer exercised.
findings.evidence: assert b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content

findings.title: KeyError when integration metadata lacks 'sender'
findings.detail: integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] is accessed unguarded. build_integration only sets 'sender' if present in state, so older or webhook-less integrations raise a KeyError and a 500 instead of a handled error.

findings.title: Token exchange request not checked and not wrapped in the try block
findings.detail: safe_urlopen is called outside the try, so network or connection errors propagate as a 500. The response status is also never checked before parsing.

findings.title: New-installation path skips identity check and relies on stale installation id
findings.detail: When no Integration exists, the flow goes to next_step without comparing the authenticated GitHub user to the installer. Any user who is authenticated with GitHub can claim an installation ID. The OAuth view also binds installation_id from an unvalidated GET parameter.

findings.title: KeyError when integration metadata lacks 'sender'
findings.detail: build_integration only stores metadata['sender'] when state has a sender. Integrations created before this change, or without the webhook sender, have no 'sender' key, so indexing raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of a handled error.

findings.title: OAuth state is the static pipeline signature and is not bound to the user
findings.detail: The state sent to GitHub is pipeline.signature, which is deterministic and appears in the URL. It is not a per-request random nonce, so it gives weak CSRF protection for the OAuth flow. An attacker who learns the signature can reuse it.

findings.title: installation_id taken from the query string without verifying the OAuth user
findings.detail: installation_id is bound to pipeline state from the request before the OAuth check. The sender check only runs when the Integration already exists; for a new Integration (DoesNotExist) the code calls next_step with no ownership check. Any user can therefore bind an arbitrary installation_id that has no Integration row yet.

findings.title: Token-exchange request and get_user_info are not guarded against errors
findings.detail: safe_urlopen is outside the try block, so network errors raise a 500. get_user_info may also raise on API errors. The broad except Exception around safe_urlread swallows everything.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the 404 path

findings.title: Shared stopped/drift cause cross-process issues; backpressure resets mask each other
findings.detail: All flusher processes share a single `stopped` and `current_drift` value, but each has its own healthy/backpressure values. Combined with `process_backpressure_since`, flushing is stopped globally while any process is backpressured; that's okay, but restarts of one process reuse shared state without isolation.

findings.title: Restart loop continues after process replacement and kill only for Process, not thread
findings.detail: On restart, a hung threading.Thread (or a hung multiprocessing process whose kill failed) is simply replaced, leaving the old thread running against the same shards and producing duplicate flushes. `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is also false for spawn-context SpawnProcess objects (they subclass BaseProcess, not the default-context `multiprocessing.Process` class), so the hung process is never killed.

findings.title: join() never terminates SpawnProcess for same isinstance bug
findings.detail: The `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` check fails for SpawnProcess created from a spawn context, so processes are never terminated in join(). Also the `break` on deadline skips terminating remaining processes entirely.

findings.title: Unused dead method and comment mismatch
findings.detail: `_create_process_for_shard` is never used, and the comment 'Update healthy_since for all shards' is misleading since healthy_since is per process.

findings.title: Test relies on time.sleep that is monkeypatched to a no-op
findings.detail: time.sleep is monkeypatched to a lambda, so the added `time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing and the test remains racy; test_flusher_processes_limit also only checks configuration, not behavior.

findings.title: Shared stopped/drift values and per-process buffers: join terminates early
findings.detail: In join(), when the deadline passes the loop `break`s before terminating remaining multiprocessing processes, so those are never terminated and remain running. Additionally, each process is terminated right after its own wait, but the break skips terminate for all later ones.

findings.title: Restart check uses isinstance on multiprocessing.Process, not SpawnProcess
findings.detail: The processes are created from a spawn context and are `SpawnProcess` instances, which are not instances of `multiprocessing.Process` (a different class from `multiprocessing.context.Process`), so isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False and hung processes are never killed before restart, leaking processes. The same wrong check in join() means terminate() is never called.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag names and high-cardinality shard tags
findings.detail: The produce timer uses tag 'shard' while wait_produce uses 'shards', making metrics inconsistent; joined shard lists as tag values also inflate cardinality.

findings.title: Test patches time.sleep then uses it to wait
findings.detail: time.sleep is monkeypatched to a no-op, so the added `time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing and the test is racy; the added limit test also never exercises flushing across processes.

findings.title: Dead code: _create_process_for_shard unused
findings.detail: The helper _create_process_for_shard is never called and the `if not process` check on a Process object is meaningless.

findings.title: Shared stopped flag / restart logic reuses shared state across processes
findings.detail: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, `process.kill()` is only called for multiprocessing.Process, but a hung thread (test mode) is never stopped and a replacement is started on the same shards, so two flushers can run concurrently on the same shards. Also `join` sets `stopped.value` once, so a restarted process after stop is immediately exited; harmless but restarts do not reset anything.

findings.title: isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process never matches SpawnProcess
findings.detail: The processes are created via a spawn context, so they are `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances, not `multiprocessing.Process` (which is the base class in `multiprocessing.process`; `multiprocessing.Process` is the same BaseProcess subclass `multiprocessing.context.Process`). SpawnProcess does not subclass `multiprocessing.Process`, so the kill and the terminate in join are likely skipped, leaving hung processes alive and leaking processes on restart.

findings.title: join breaks out of loop without terminating remaining processes
findings.detail: When the deadline expires, the loop `break`s and the remaining processes are never terminated, leaving orphan flusher processes. Also the check `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` may not match SpawnProcess.

findings.title: Unused/dead helper and buffers dict inconsistent after restart
findings.detail: `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code. Restarting a process creates a new SpansBuffer and replaces the old one in `self.buffers`, fine, but the old process is not guaranteed killed (see isinstance issue), so old buffer state/connection remains in use by the hung process.

findings.title: Restart limit check off-by-one and docstring mismatch
findings.detail: Docstring says one process per shard, but processes are capped by max_processes (default 1 from CLI), so shards share processes. Also the CLI default of 1 collapses all shards into a single process, silently changing previous behavior semantic from `None` meaning one per shard.
findings.evidence: Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.

findings.detail: `time.sleep` is monkeypatched to a lambda, so the `time.sleep(0.1)` added to wait for flusher threads does nothing and the test remains racy.

findings.title: Worker blocks forever on get() and ignores shutdown flag
findings.detail: OrderedQueueWorker.run calls work_queue.get() with no timeout. `shutdown` is only checked when looping. queue.ShutDown exists only in Python 3.13+, so on older Pythons the `except queue.ShutDown` raises AttributeError and `q.shutdown()` is missing, leaving workers hanging.

findings.title: Offset commit state mishandled when worker exits on ShutDown
findings.detail: When the queue is shut down mid-processing, the worker breaks. The `finally` still runs, completing the offset even though the item may not have been processed. After shutdown(immediate=False), get() raises ShutDown only once the queue is drained, but the shutdown flag set earlier makes the loop exit and drops queued items without processing or completing their offsets.

Conversely, the first call with last_committed=-1 can commit past offsets not yet submitted, since only in-flight offsets are known.

findings.title: Python hash() of str is randomized per process
findings.detail: hash(group_key) is salted by PYTHONHASHSEED, so the group-to-queue mapping differs between processes/restarts. Within a single process ordering holds, but the 'consistent hashing' docstring is misleading and the mapping is non-reproducible.

findings.title: Processing failures and submit errors are committed as success; no backpressure
findings.detail: On submit exception the offset is marked complete, silently dropping the message, contradicting the docstring 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and 'Natural backpressure' (queues are unbounded, so submit never blocks). Rebalance also never clears tracker state or flushes commits on close.

findings.title: Commit performed from background thread on shared Kafka commit callback
findings.detail: The commit function from arroyo is invoked from a separate thread, not the consumer's poll thread; arroyo's commit is not thread-safe. Also the strategy's close() joins without a final commit of remaining completed offsets, and the loop waits before checking so the last commit may be lost.

findings.detail: get_committable_offsets requires strictly contiguous offsets (+1), but Kafka offsets on a topic can have gaps (compaction, transactions, filtered messages not tracked). Also, with last_committed=-1 it starts at min_offset, so offsets never submitted below it are assumed committed. After a gap the commit stalls forever. A rebalance also leaves stale state.

findings.title: Commit thread commits offsets for revoked partitions / no rebalance handling
findings.detail: A background thread calls the arroyo commit function outside the consumer's poll thread, and the strategy's shared FixedQueuePool/OffsetTracker persists across create_with_partitions calls and rebalances. Strategy close() shuts down the shared pool, so after a rebalance a new strategy gets a dead pool (queues shut down, workers stopped), and stale offsets can be committed for partitions no longer owned.

findings.title: Unbounded queues contradict claimed backpressure; failed items still committed
findings.detail: Docstring promises natural backpressure and commit only after successful processing, but queues are unbounded (queue.Queue()) so submit never blocks, and the worker's finally block completes offsets even when processing raised, so failed messages get committed.

findings.detail: The test claims errors don't block offset commits but asserts no commit happened (len==0 or partition not in committed_offsets), which contradicts its docstring and, because the commit loop runs once per second, the check is timing-dependent.

findings.detail: get_committable_offsets stops at the first offset not present in all_offsets. Offsets can have gaps from compaction, transaction markers, or the filtered/skipped messages arroyo doesn't deliver. findings.title: Offsets pruned after commit; later start computed from last_committed+1 causes stall
findings.detail: After commit, all_offsets is pruned and the scan starts at last_committed+1. If the next delivered offset is greater than last_committed+1 (any gap, or after a partition rebalance), the loop breaks at the first iteration and never commits again.

findings.title: Worker loop can drop queued items on shutdown and ignores partition revocation
findings.detail: The worker's shutdown flag is checked in the loop condition, so after pool.shutdown() sets it, workers exit while items remain queued; those are never processed and never completed. The strategy also never clears state on rebalance, and close() doesn't drain, so unprocessed offsets are lost or stale offsets are committed for revoked partitions.

findings.title: Claims of backpressure and success-only commits are untrue
findings.detail: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure, and submit never blocks. Offsets are completed in a finally block even when processing raises, so failed items are committed, contradicting 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'.

findings.title: Denial cache is never invalidated and blocks newly granted permissions
findings.detail: A denial is cached for the (user, action, name, folder) tuple and checked before the permission cache or the DB. For its TTL, a permission granted in the meantime is still denied, which defeats the 'Fallback to the database on outdated cache' behaviour added for allows. Renderer and anonymous identities are also cached this way.

findings.title: Denial cache key is ambiguous and collides with the permission cache key space
findings.detail: Fields are joined with '_' and no escaping, and the key shares the 'perm_<uid>_<action>' prefix with userPermCacheKey. Names or folders containing underscores can collide, e.g. name 'a_b' with folder 'c' versus name 'a' with folder 'b_c'. A cached denial for one resource could then wrongly deny another. The key also uses the raw request userUID rather than the resolved UID.
findings.evidence: return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent

findings.title: Cached-permission error in Check short-circuits fallback; metrics double-counted
findings.detail: An error from checkPermission on cached perms (e.g. folder tree lookup failure) returns immediately instead of falling back to the DB path. In addition, the cache-usage metric is incremented 'true' on a cache-allow and 'false' on every other path, including a denial from the cache, so metrics are misleading.

findings.title: Denial cache never invalidated; denials persist after permission grants
findings.detail: A denial is cached for 30s per user/action/name/folder. Because the denial lookup runs before any other check, a permission granted during that window is still denied. This undermines the 'fall back to DB on outdated cache' behaviour that the allow path implements.

findings.title: Denial cache key built from unescaped concatenation allows collisions
findings.detail: The key joins action, name and parent with '_' without escaping. Names or folders containing underscores can collide, e.g. name 'a_b'/parent 'c' versus name 'a'/parent 'b_c'. A cached denial for one resource can then wrongly deny another. The key also shares the 'perm_<uid>_<action>' prefix with userPermCacheKey, so it can collide with the permission cache key space.
findings.evidence: return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent

findings.title: Denial cache key uses raw UserUID, and the lookup precedes identity resolution
findings.detail: The denial key uses the raw subject ID from the request. The permission cache key uses the resolved userIdentifiers.UID, and the idCache is keyed by both UID and numeric ID. The same user referenced by different identifiers therefore gets different denial entries, so the denial cache is inconsistent with the permission cache.

findings.title: Negative decisions cached under a key that never gets invalidated by permission changes
findings.detail: A denied check is stored in permDenialCache for the short TTL and consulted before the permission cache, so a grant made after a denial is ignored until the entry expires. The denial check also overrides the fresh DB fallback that this PR adds for outdated caches. This makes newly granted access stay denied and creates stale-authorization behavior.

findings.title: Denial cache key collides with permission cache key namespace and is ambiguous
findings.detail: The denial key has the prefix namespace.perm_<uid>_<action> identical to userPermCacheKey, with name/parent appended using '_' separators. Names or folders containing '_' can collide with other combinations, and a different action name could collide with the base key. This can poison a cache entry and produce wrong denials.
findings.evidence: return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent

findings.title: Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds and races

For file-backed indexes bleve.New on the same directory fails for the second builder, and the last one overwrites the cache entry, leaking the other. findings.title: Shared err and counter mutated from errgroup goroutines

findings.title: Init now runs with watcher context before server is usable; failure leaks resources

findings.title: BuildIndex no longer serialized; concurrent builds for same key race
