findings.detail: The regex `_[a-zA-Z-_]*\.properties` can match from an earlier underscore in the path (e.g. directory names), and a missing English file throws a RuntimeException instead of being reported. Files that have no `_en` counterpart break the whole verification.

findings.title: Reader thread is never joined and may outlive the test
findings.detail: The background reader thread is started and never joined. The test asserts on caughtExceptions right after setting the flag, so an exception thrown by a still-running read is missed, and the thread can keep calling the admin client after the test (and the realm) are torn down.

findings.title: Test can pass without having exercised any concurrent read/delete overlap
findings.detail: There is no synchronization to ensure the reader thread has started or completed at least one read before deletion begins. The thread may also be slow to start, so deletions can finish before any read happens. The test can then pass without hitting the race it targets.

findings.title: getSubGroupsCount returns null for deleted group, callers may NPE
findings.detail: When the underlying group no longer exists the method now returns null. Callers such as GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount pass the value straight to setSubGroupCount, which works for a Long. Other callers may unbox the result. Returning null silently hides the deletion instead of a clear signal.

findings.title: Reader thread not joined; test can finish before or race with it
findings.detail: The background thread is started but never joined after `deletedAll` is set. The assertion on `caughtExceptions` may run before the reader's last iteration completes, so late exceptions are missed. The thread can also keep calling the admin client after the test (and realm cleanup) ends, causing flakiness.

findings.title: Test never verifies the reader thread actually ran
findings.detail: There is no check that the reader performed any reads while deletes were happening. A fast delete loop can finish before the thread does any work, so the test would pass without exercising the race it targets.

findings.title: Assertion failure inside lambda and shared non-thread-safe list
findings.detail: The group IDs are collected in a plain ArrayList from within a forEach lambda, and `fail()` is called inside a try-with-resources block. The test would be clearer and safer with a plain loop. Failures in the deletion loop also leave the reader thread spinning forever, because `deletedAll` is never set when an exception is thrown.

findings.title: Reader thread is not joined and may outlive the test
findings.detail: The background thread is started and never joined. After deletedAll is set, assertions run immediately, so an exception in an in-flight read can be missed, making the test flaky and unable to reliably catch the race. The thread can also keep running into later tests.

findings.title: Non-volatile-safe loop with no pacing and unbounded request flood
findings.detail: The reader loops with no delay or limit, issuing repeated Integer.MAX_VALUE-sized requests while the main thread deletes groups. This can overload the server and slow the test. If the delete loop throws, deletedAll is never set and the thread spins forever.

findings.title: ES384/ES512 tests sign with a P-256 key
findings.detail: The key pair is created with the default EC curve (secp256r1) for every test. The ES384 and ES512 cases therefore only produce 32-byte r/s values that get padded to 48 or 66 bytes. Full-width values and the leading-zero sign-byte handling at those sizes are never exercised. The round-trip comparison also cannot catch a wrong encoding that is symmetric.

findings.title: Dead redundant encoding calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.detail: The results of the two standalone ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls are discarded. They duplicate the encoding done in the return statement and do pointless work.

findings.title: Indefinite length (-1) not handled in readInteger/readNext
findings.detail: readLength returns -1 for the indefinite-length marker 0x80. readInteger passes it straight to read(-1), which throws NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException. A malformed signature can therefore trigger an unchecked exception.

findings.title: ES384/ES512 tests use the default EC key, not the matching curve
findings.detail: One default-size EC key pair (typically P-256) is used for ES256, ES384 and ES512, so the signature size does not match the signLength passed for ES384 or ES512. The test only checks a self-consistent round trip, so it misses encoding bugs for real P-384/P-521 signatures such as 66-byte values or length-form encoding.

findings.title: Malformed DER input can throw unchecked exceptions instead of IOException
findings.detail: readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, and readInteger passes it to read(length), which allocates new byte[-1] and throws NegativeArraySizeException. A zero-length INTEGER also reaches new BigInteger(empty) and throws NumberFormatException. A crafted signature therefore escapes the declared IOException contract.

findings.title: integerToBytes silently truncates oversized r/s values
findings.detail: When the DER integer is longer than qLength, the leading bytes are dropped without checking they are only the sign-padding zero. An invalid oversized r or s is therefore accepted as a different value, which allows signature malleability instead of rejecting the input.

findings.title: Dead redundant ASN.1 encoding calls
findings.detail: Two ASN1Encoder instances are created and encoded and the results discarded, then the same values are encoded again for the returned sequence. This is useless work and looks like leftover debugging code.

findings.title: Ambiguous providers no longer rejected; ties in order() resolve arbitrarily
findings.detail: The multiple-provider error is removed, and the default, Elytron and FIPS providers all return order() 200. If more than one is on the classpath, the winner depends on ServiceLoader ordering and is only visible in debug logs, where startup previously failed fast.

findings.title: Oversized R/S values are silently truncated when decoding a DER signature
findings.detail: When the decoded integer has more bytes than signLength/2, integerToBytes keeps only the low-order bytes instead of rejecting it. A malformed or oversized signature component is turned into a different value without any error.

findings.title: Dead encoder calls that discard their results
findings.detail: Two ASN1Encoder.write(...) calls produce encoders that are never used. They are leftover code and do redundant work.

findings.title: Indefinite or negative length causes NegativeArraySizeException or silently empty result
findings.detail: readLength returns -1 for the indefinite-length form 0x80. readInteger and readNext then call read(-1), which throws NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException. readSequence silently returns an empty list for that length.

findings.title: isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted grant check and wrong substring range
findings.detail: The matcher returns false when the grant shortcut equals the expected one, so it rejects correct tokens and accepts wrong ones. The grant shortcut is at chars 4-5 (substring(4,6)), not substring(3,5), which covers the last char of the token type and the first char of the grant.

findings.title: rawTokenId null check validates grantType instead
findings.detail: The null check intended for rawTokenId is applied to grantType again, so a null rawTokenId is accepted. The encoded token id would then contain the literal string 'null'.

findings.title: Duplicate shortcut validation can miss collisions and uses overwritten entries
findings.detail: Duplicates are detected only by comparing map sizes after puts that silently overwrite. A collision with another grant's shortcut, or with the 'na' unknown shortcut, can go undetected, and the size check can still pass when the collisions cancel out.

findings.title: isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted/wrong grant shortcut check
findings.detail: The matcher returns false when the grant shortcut EQUALS the expected one, which is inverted. The substring(3,5) offsets are also wrong: the grant shortcut sits at indices 4-6 (substring(4,6)), so the check never compares the right characters.

findings.title: rawTokenId null check validates grantType instead
findings.detail: The null check labelled for rawTokenId is applied to grantType, so a null rawTokenId is accepted and later encoded as the string 'null'.

findings.title: Lightweight detection uses session context client rather than the token's client
findings.detail: Token type is derived from session.getContext().getClient() via getShouldUseLightweightToken, which may differ from the client passed to initToken (e.g. token exchange, refresh) and NPEs when no client is set in context.

findings.title: Unused import added
findings.detail: TokenExchangeGrantTypeFactory is imported but unused, and the shortcut is not used here; the GRANT_TYPE constant is set with a hardcoded value instead.

findings.title: isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted and off-by-one grant shortcut check
findings.detail: The grant shortcut is at chars 4-5 (substring(4,6)), but the code uses substring(3,5). It also returns false when the shortcut EQUALS the expected one, so the matcher rejects correct token IDs and accepts wrong ones.

findings.title: rawTokenId null check validates grantType instead
findings.detail: The requireNonNull for rawTokenId checks grantType, so a null rawTokenId is accepted and would be encoded as the string 'null'.

findings.title: Cleanup removes literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDP
findings.detail: The cleanup registered in the creation loop targets an IDP whose alias is the literal string "alias", not the one just created. The 20+ IDPs created by testCacheIDPForLogin are therefore never cleaned up and can leak into later tests.

findings.title: Update invalidation uses org-aware wrapped model, so cached login lists can go stale
findings.detail: `original` comes from `getById`, which wraps the model so `isEnabled()` is false whenever the owning org or the org feature is disabled. The cached login lists are built from the raw DB state. An update that hides or disables such an IDP is then treated as 'not login before and after', and no invalidation happens, leaving the IDP in the cached list.

findings.title: Cleanup registered with literal "alias" instead of the created IDP alias
findings.detail: The cleanup callback removes the IDP whose alias is the literal string "alias", not the one just created. The 21 IDPs created by the test are never cleaned up and can leak into other tests.

findings.title: Cleanup removes literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDP
findings.detail: The cleanup handler calls `identityProviders().get("alias")::remove`, but no IDP has the alias "alias". The 21 IDPs the test creates are never cleaned up and can leak into other tests, and the cleanup itself may fail with a 404.

findings.title: remove() now always queries the delegate and may pass a null IDP to registerIDPInvalidation
findings.detail: `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` now runs on every remove, even when the IDP is already cached and the value is unused, which adds a DB lookup. If the alias does not exist, `storedIdp` is null and the invalid-key branch calls `registerIDPInvalidation(null)`, which throws an NPE.

findings.title: Login predicate now also requires org-linked IDPs to be public, contradicting the getForLogin javadoc
findings.detail: `getLoginPredicate` now excludes org-linked IDPs unless BROKER_PUBLIC is true. The `getForLogin` javadoc and the LoginFilter enum only list enabled, not link-only and not hidden as the criteria. This silently changes the semantics for other callers of `getLoginPredicate`.

findings.title: canManage() grants group management on the VIEW scope
findings.detail: canManage() with no group argument accepts the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource. An admin with only view permission on all groups passes requireManage() and can create top-level groups. The interface Javadoc has the same mistake.

findings.title: Resource id is used where the group id is expected
findings.detail: Group permission resources are named by group id, but the code passes groupResource.getId() (the resource UUID) to hasPermission(), which looks up by name. The lookup misses and falls back to the all-groups resource, so the evaluation targets the wrong resource. The set returned also contains resource ids instead of group ids. findByType also returns the generic 'Groups' type resource, which is not a real group.

findings.title: Javadoc says Stream but the method returns Set; canManage doc lists VIEW
findings.detail: The Javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a Stream, but the method returns Set<String>. The canManage() Javadoc also claims VIEW grants management, which matches the faulty V2 implementation.
findings.evidence: * @return Stream of IDs of groups with view permission.

findings.title: canManage() grants manage on the VIEW scope
findings.detail: canManage() calls hasPermission with both VIEW and MANAGE. An admin granted only the view scope on all groups therefore passes canManage() and requireManage(), so create-group and similar operations are allowed with view-only permission.

findings.title: Resource id used where group id (resource name) is expected
findings.detail: Group resources are named by group id, and hasPermission looks them up with findByName. The code passes and collects groupResource.getId(), which is the resource UUID. The lookup misses, falls back to the all-groups resource, and the returned set holds resource UUIDs rather than group ids. The user search filter by group membership then matches nothing or the wrong groups.

findings.title: Granted scopes not tied to the evaluated resource
findings.detail: The evaluator returns every permission, and the loop accepts a matching scope from any of them. It does not check that permission.getResourceId() equals resource.getId(), as UserPermissionsV2 does. A matching scope granted on another resource can authorize access to this group.

findings.title: canManage() grants global manage on groups for VIEW-only permission
findings.detail: canManage() checks the VIEW scope in addition to MANAGE on the all-groups resource. An admin who is only allowed to view all groups passes requireManage() and can create groups, update them and map roles.

findings.title: Resource UUID used instead of group id when collecting viewable groups
findings.detail: Group resources are named after the group id, and hasPermission() looks them up with findByName. groupResource.getId() is the resource's internal UUID, so the lookup misses and falls back to the all-groups resource. The set also ends up holding resource UUIDs instead of group ids, which breaks the user search group filter. Use groupResource.getName() instead.

findings.title: Evaluated permissions are not filtered by the resource being checked
findings.detail: hasPermission() accepts any returned permission whose scopes match, without comparing permission.getResourceId() to the resource. UserPermissionsV2 does make this check. Permissions that apply to other resources could be treated as granting access to this group.

findings.title: Federated recovery codes consumption never persisted; removal targets wrong store
findings.detail: The credential is now fetched from federated storage too, but marking codes used is not stored back. When all codes are used, `removeStoredCredentialById` is called with a federated credential id, which is not a local credential. The exhausted federated credential persists, so the user is not prompted to set up new codes. Federated codes are also reusable.

findings.title: Unchecked Optional.get() can throw NoSuchElementException
findings.detail: The result of getCredential is dereferenced with get() without checking presence. If neither store has the credential (for example a federated provider whose getCredentials does not return it), rendering the login form fails with an unhandled exception.

findings.title: Recovery codes model built from raw codes, not hashed; used-state never tracked
findings.detail: getCredentials rebuilds the model with createFromValues on the stored raw JSON list, so the codes are never marked as used. isValid compares raw codes with equals against the input, and the plaintext codes are stored. Validation is not hash-based like the real provider, and the consumed-code flow is not exercised.

findings.title: getCredentials dereferences possibly-null MyUser
findings.detail: getMyUser returns null for unknown users, and myUser.recoveryCodes is accessed immediately. Other methods in the class guard against null, so this causes an NPE.

findings.title: Federated recovery credential removed via local-store API when all codes used
findings.detail: The credential can now come from user storage, but the exhausted-codes cleanup still calls removeStoredCredentialById. That only touches the local DB and does not remove or update the federated credential. Federated credentials also never get their used-code state persisted.

findings.title: Unchecked Optional.get() on credential lookup
findings.detail: The new lookup may return an empty Optional, for example when the user storage does not return the credential via getFederatedCredentialsStream. Calling get() throws NoSuchElementException and breaks the login form.

findings.title: Recovery codes stored as raw plaintext in user storage
findings.detail: The raw (unhashed) recovery codes are serialised to JSON and handed to the user storage provider via updateCredential. Locally the codes are hashed in credentialModel, so the storage path is inconsistent and exposes valid secrets to external providers.
findings.evidence: UserCredentialModel recoveryCodesCredential = new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson);

findings.title: getCredentials rebuilds recovery credential and loses stored id
findings.detail: The recovery model is re-created via createFromValues, which hashes the codes again and generates a new id. The id stored on myUser.recoveryCodes is lost and the model can't match stored data. Also, a deserialization failure is only logged and the exception is swallowed.

findings.title: Federated recovery credential is not removed or updated after use
findings.detail: getCredential can now return a federated credential, but the code then calls removeStoredCredentialById on it when all codes are used. That method only removes local DB credentials, so a federated credential is never deleted. The user-storage-side isValid also never consumes a used code, so recovery codes are reusable.

findings.title: Plain recovery codes serialized and sent to user storage; wrapped in generic RuntimeException
findings.detail: The raw recovery codes are serialized to JSON and handed to arbitrary user storage providers in clear text instead of hashed values. The IOException is rethrown as a bare RuntimeException, which loses context.

findings.title: getCredentials dereferences possibly null user and ignores credential type filter
findings.detail: getMyUser may return null for an unknown user, and myUser.recoveryCodes is then accessed without a null check, causing an NPE. Other methods in this class guard against null.
